question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Obstinate
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Stubborn.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Obstinate" means stubbornly refusing to change one's opinion or chosen course of action, despite attempts to persuade one to do so. (ज़िद्दी)
◦ Example: The obstinate child refused to eat his vegetables no matter how much his mother pleaded.

• "Stubborn" is a close synonym of "Obstinate", meaning having or showing dogged determination not to change one's attitude or position on something, hence Option 3 is correct.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Obedient" (आज्ञाकारी): Willing to comply with the wishes of one in authority; this is opposite in meaning to "Obstinate".

• Option 2: "Adaptive" (अनुकूलनीय): Able to adjust to new conditions; unrelated to stubbornness.

• Option 4: "Submissive" (विनम्र/आज्ञाकारी): Ready to conform to the authority or will of others; again opposite in sense to "Obstinate".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "Obstinate" frequently asked in SSC exams: Adamant, Headstrong, Inflexible, Stubborn, Intransigent, Unyielding.

• Antonyms of "Obstinate" include: Docile, Compliant, Flexible, Amenable.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Left out in the cold
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. To be ignored.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Left out in the cold" means to be ignored, excluded or neglected by others, especially from a group activity, decision or social situation. (उपेक्षित/अलग-थलग छोड़ दिया जाना)
◦ Example: When the new project team was formed, he felt left out in the cold as no one informed him about the meetings.

• The idiom draws on the image of being kept outside, away from the warmth of a fire or shelter, and hence excluded from comfort and company.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "To go underground" (भूमिगत हो जाना): To hide from authorities or go into concealment, usually to escape detection.

• Option 2: "To be in hiding": To stay concealed from others; this describes physical concealment, not being ignored.

• Option 4: "To be extremely negative": Refers to a pessimistic attitude, unrelated to the idiom's meaning of exclusion.

NOTE

• Other idioms of exclusion/neglect often asked in SSC: "To give someone the cold shoulder" (to deliberately ignore someone), "To be sidelined", and "To be given short shrift" (to be dismissed with little consideration).

question:
Parts of a sentence are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the parts in the correct order to form a meaningful sentence.
P. and has also created a wide gap between them
Q. laid too much stress on
R. teachers and students
S. online mode of education has
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. SQRP.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence must begin with the subject and verb that introduce the main idea, so it starts with S ("online mode of education has"), which needs a main verb-phrase to follow.

• S is followed by Q ("laid too much stress on"), since "has" requires the past participle "laid" to complete the verb phrase "has laid".

• Q is followed by R ("teachers and students"), as "laid too much stress on" needs an object, which is "teachers and students".

• R is followed by P ("and has also created a wide gap between them"), which adds a second, connected consequence using "and has also created", with "them" referring back to "teachers and students".

• Combining in this order gives: "Online mode of education has laid too much stress on teachers and students and has also created a wide gap between them."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: SRPQ is incorrect because it places "teachers and students" directly after "online mode of education has", producing the meaningless string "online mode of education has teachers and students".

• Option 2: RQPS is incorrect because it begins with "teachers and students", which cannot logically start the sentence without a preceding subject-verb structure.

• Option 4: PSQR is incorrect because it begins with "and", which cannot start a standalone sentence, and disrupts the logical subject-verb-object flow.

NOTE

• In parajumble questions, always look for the part that contains the main subject to begin the sentence, and check for linking words like "and", "but", "which" to identify parts that must follow another specific part.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
A thing that can be easily carried by hands
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Portable.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Portable" means a thing that can be easily carried by hands or moved from one place to another. (आसानी से हाथ से ले जाने योग्य)
◦ Example: She bought a portable speaker that she could carry to the park.

• The word comes from the Latin "portare", meaning "to carry", which also gives us related words like "transport" and "porter".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Export" (निर्यात करना): To send goods or services to another country for sale.

• Option 2: "Import" (आयात करना): To bring in goods or services from another country.

• Option 3: "Potable" (पीने योग्य): Safe to drink; refers to water fit for drinking, not something carried by hand.

NOTE

• Do not confuse "Potable" (drinkable) with "Portable" (carriable) — they are frequently confused in SSC one-word substitution questions due to their similar spelling.

• Other useful one-word substitutions: "Legible" (that which can be read easily), "Audible" (that which can be heard), "Edible" (that which can be eaten).

question:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains an error.
He always wants to be in the company of those who are intellectually superior than him.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. superior than him.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The adjective "superior" is a Latin comparative form, and such words are always followed by "to", not "than", to make a comparison.

• Rule: Certain comparative adjectives of Latin origin — superior, inferior, junior, senior, prior, preferable — take "to" instead of "than" when comparing two things or persons.

• Applying the rule, the phrase "superior than him" must be corrected to "superior to him".

• Corrected sentence: "He always wants to be in the company of those who are intellectually superior to him."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "be in the company of" is grammatically correct as it stands and contains no error.

• Option 3: "He always wants to" is grammatically correct; the subject-verb agreement ("He...wants") is proper for third person singular.

• Option 4: "those who are intellectually" is correct as written; "those who" correctly introduces a relative clause.

NOTE

• Other Latin comparatives that take "to" instead of "than": anterior to, posterior to, superior to, inferior to, junior to, senior to, prior to, preferable to.

• Example: "Ravi is senior to Mohan" (NOT "senior than Mohan").

question:
Parts of a sentence are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the parts in the correct order to form a meaningful sentence.
O. want
P. movie tonight
Q. do you
R. to watch
S. the
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. QORSP.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence is a question, so it should begin with the auxiliary verb followed by the subject: Q ("do you").

• Q is followed by O ("want"), giving "do you want", which is the correct verb form after the auxiliary "do".

• O is followed by R ("to watch"), since "want" is typically followed by an infinitive: "want to watch".

• R is followed by S ("the") and then P ("movie tonight"), giving the object "the movie tonight".

• Combining in this order gives: "Do you want to watch the movie tonight?"

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: RSPQO is incorrect because it begins with "to watch", which cannot start an interrogative sentence.

• Option 3: OSQPR is incorrect because it begins with "want", producing the ungrammatical opening "Want the do you...".

• Option 4: OSPQR is incorrect for the same reason — it begins with "want", disrupting the required auxiliary-subject-verb order of a question.

NOTE

• Interrogative sentences formed with "do/does/did" always follow the pattern: Auxiliary + Subject + Base Verb + Object/Complement + ?

• Example structure: "Do + you + want + to watch + the movie tonight?"

question:
Parts of a sentence are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the parts in the correct order to form a meaningful sentence.
P) always favours
Q) only the
R) fortune
S) bold
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. RPQS.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence is based on the well-known proverb "Fortune favours the bold", modified here with "only", so it must begin with the subject R ("fortune").

• R is followed by P ("always favours"), giving "fortune always favours", which forms the subject-verb combination.

• P is followed by Q ("only the") and then S ("bold"), giving the object phrase "only the bold".

• Combining in this order gives: "Fortune always favours only the bold."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: SQPR is incorrect as it begins with "bold", which cannot logically start the sentence.

• Option 3: SRQP is incorrect for the same reason — it begins with "bold", disrupting the subject-verb-object order.

• Option 4: PQRS is incorrect because it begins with the verb phrase "always favours" without a subject, producing an ungrammatical opening.

NOTE

• The full original proverb is "Fortune favours the bold/brave", meaning that people who take risks are more likely to succeed than those who are cautious.

• Always identify the grammatical subject of a sentence first when solving parajumbles — it usually anchors the correct starting part.

question:
Parts of a sentence are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the parts in the correct order to form a meaningful sentence.
A. Only for themselves
B. Is full of
C. People who live
D. The world
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. DBCA.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence must begin with the subject, which is D ("The world").

• D is followed by B ("Is full of"), giving "The world is full of", the subject-verb-preposition combination.

• B is followed by C ("People who live"), since "is full of" needs an object, which is "people who live...".

• C is followed by A ("Only for themselves"), completing the relative clause "people who live only for themselves".

• Combining in this order gives: "The world is full of people who live only for themselves."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: BCAD is incorrect because it begins with the verb phrase "Is full of" without a subject.

• Option 2: ABCD is incorrect because it begins with "Only for themselves", which cannot logically start the sentence.

• Option 3: DBAC is incorrect because it places "Only for themselves" before "People who live", producing the illogical order "is full of only for themselves people who live".

NOTE

• In parajumbles, a relative clause beginning with "who", "which", "that" must always directly follow the noun it describes — here, "who live only for themselves" must follow "People".

• Always check that the final combined sentence makes complete logical and grammatical sense before finalising the order.

question:
Select the option that correctly expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
Mr. Amar refused him admittance.
option_1: Admittance will be refused to him by Mr. Amar.
option_2: Admittance shall be refused to him by Mr. Amar.
option_3: Admittance would be refused to him by Mr. Amar.
option_4: Admittance was refused to him by Mr. Amar.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Admittance was refused to him by Mr. Amar.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "Mr. Amar refused him admittance" is in the Simple Past Tense.

• Rule — Simple Past Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + V2 + Object
◦ Passive: Object + was/were + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the direct object "admittance" becomes the subject; the auxiliary used for past tense with a singular/uncountable noun is "was"; the verb "refused" (already V2/V3 same form) remains as the past participle; the indirect object "him" is retained after "to"; and "Mr. Amar" becomes the agent introduced by "by".
◦ Passive: Admittance was refused to him by Mr. Amar.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "will be refused" is the passive form of the Simple Future Tense, not the Simple Past Tense used in the original sentence.

• Option 2 is incorrect because "shall be refused" is also a future-tense passive construction, inconsistent with the past tense verb "refused" in the active sentence.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "would be refused" expresses a conditional or reported past-future sense, not the direct Simple Past Tense of the original.

NOTE

• When a ditransitive verb (like "refuse", "give", "offer") takes two objects, the indirect object typically becomes the subject of the passive sentence, but with "refuse", the direct object (the thing refused) is generally preferred as the subject, and the indirect object follows with "to".

• Example: "They offered him a job" → Passive: "He was offered a job" OR "A job was offered to him."

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Break the ice
option_2: Ill-feeling carried by a person over a period of time
option_4: To say or do something that makes people feel more relaxed, especially at the beginning of a meeting, party
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. To say or do something that makes people feel more relaxed, especially at the beginning of a meeting, party.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Break the ice" means to say or do something that relieves tension or awkwardness, especially when people meet for the first time or at the start of an event. (माहौल को सहज बनाना)
◦ Example: The host told a funny joke to break the ice at the start of the party.

• The idiom originates from the practice of ships breaking through ice to allow passage, symbolising the clearing away of an initial barrier to communication.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Nervousness before a performance" describes stage fright, which is unrelated to the idiom's meaning.

• Option 2: "Ill-feeling carried by a person over a period of time" describes holding a grudge, which is the opposite of easing tension.

• Option 3: "Respect for someone's achievements" describes admiration, which has no connection to easing social awkwardness.

NOTE

• Other idioms related to social interaction often asked in SSC: "To hit it off" (to become friendly quickly), "To make small talk" (to converse about unimportant matters casually), and "To warm up to someone" (to gradually become friendly).

question:
Select the most appropriate homophone to fill in the blank.
The summer was ______ hot this year.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. too.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a word meaning "excessively" or "also", used here to intensify the adjective "hot".

• "Too" means to a higher degree than is acceptable, or excessively, and is correctly used before an adjective as in "too hot".

• Completed sentence: "The summer was too hot this year."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "tow" means to pull a vehicle or object using a rope or chain; it does not fit the sentence grammatically or contextually.

• Option 2: "two" is the number 2; it cannot be used to intensify an adjective like "hot".

• Option 3: "to" is a preposition or infinitive marker; it cannot precede an adjective to show degree in this context.

NOTE

• Homophones are words that sound alike but differ in spelling and meaning. Commonly confused triads in SSC exams: to / too / two, there / their / they're, its / it's, hear / here.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the bracketed word in the following sentence to fill in the blank.
The mothers, who suffer from postpartum depression, feel ______ by their children. (vexed)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. annoyed.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The bracketed word "vexed" means annoyed, irritated or troubled. (चिढ़ा हुआ/परेशान)
◦ Example: She felt vexed when her plans were cancelled at the last minute.

• "Annoyed" is the closest synonym, correctly conveying the sense of irritation or distress felt by mothers suffering from postpartum depression.

• Completed sentence: "The mothers, who suffer from postpartum depression, feel annoyed by their children."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "delighted" (प्रसन्न): Means extremely pleased, which is opposite in meaning to "vexed".

• Option 2: "recovered" (स्वस्थ हुआ): Means to have regained health, unrelated to the meaning of "vexed".

• Option 3: "pacific" (शांत): Means calm or peaceful, which is the opposite of "vexed".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "vexed": irritated, exasperated, provoked, irked, annoyed, agitated.

• Antonyms of "vexed": pleased, content, calm, satisfied.

question:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains an error.
I have sing 'Let It Go' before a crowd of thousands of people.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. I have sing.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence uses the Present Perfect Tense, formed with has/have + past participle (V3).

• Rule: After the auxiliary "have/has", the main verb must always be in its past participle (V3) form, not the base form (V1).

• The base form "sing" is incorrectly used after "have"; it must be replaced with its past participle "sung".

• Corrected sentence: "I have sung 'Let It Go' before a crowd of thousands of people."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "a crowd of" is grammatically correct and needs no change.

• Option 2: "thousands of people" is a correctly formed plural noun phrase and contains no error.

• Option 4: "'Let It Go' before" is correctly used to introduce the object of the sentence and the following prepositional phrase.

NOTE

• Common irregular verb forms confused in this way: sing–sang–sung, go–went–gone, do–did–done, see–saw–seen, write–wrote–written.

• Always check that a base-form verb (V1) is never used directly after "has/have/had" — the correct form is always the past participle (V3).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
Aesthetic value is specifically a way in which we can get positive conclude value from the world at large.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. can get positive conclusive value.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined phrase uses "conclude", a verb, in a position where an adjective is grammatically required to modify the noun "value".

• The correct adjective form is "conclusive", meaning serving to prove a point or put an end to doubt; decisive and definite. (निर्णायक)
◦ Example: The DNA test provided conclusive value in solving the case.

• Replacing "conclude" with "conclusive" gives the grammatically correct and meaningful phrase: "can get positive conclusive value".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "convalescent" (स्वास्थ्यलाभ संबंधी): Relating to recovery from illness; contextually meaningless here.

• Option 2: "convulsive" (ऐंठनयुक्त): Relating to sudden, uncontrollable muscle contractions; unrelated to the intended meaning.

• Option 4: "contrastive" (विरोधाभासी): Relating to a notable difference between things being compared; does not fit the intended positive sense.

NOTE

• Be careful of words with similar spellings but very different meanings: conclude (verb) vs. conclusive (adjective), convince (verb) vs. convincing (adjective).

• Always check whether the blank/underlined position requires a noun, verb, or adjective before choosing the replacement word.

question:
Select the correctly spelt word to fill in the blank.
My grandmother ________________ the preparation of every festival celebration in my house.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. initiates.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "initiates" — meaning causes a process or action to begin.
◦ Example: The teacher initiates every class with a short revision of the previous lesson.

• Spelling key: I + NI + TI + ATES. Note the sequence "in" followed by "iti" and the ending "-ates". The word comes from the Latin initiare, meaning "to begin".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "inetiates" — incorrect; the letters "n" and "e" have been wrongly interchanged after "i".

• Option 3: "enitiates" — incorrect; the word wrongly begins with "en-" instead of "in-".

• Option 4: "enetiates" — incorrect; it combines both errors, beginning with "en-" and misplacing the "e".

NOTE

• Related word forms: initiate (verb/noun), initiation (noun), initiative (noun), initial (adjective).

• Other commonly misspelt words with the "in-" prefix: innovate, initiate, inhibit, ingenious.

question:
In the question, four alternatives are given for the underlined word in the sentence. Choose the alternative which best expresses the opposite meaning of the word.
It was as if the newer hybrids had an insatiable appetite for chemicals.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Satisfiable.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined word "insatiable" means impossible to satisfy; having an appetite or desire that can never be fully satisfied. (अतृप्त)
◦ Example: He had an insatiable curiosity about how machines worked.

• The antonym "Satisfiable" means capable of being satisfied, which is directly opposite to "insatiable".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Urgent" (अत्यावश्यक): Requiring immediate attention; unrelated to the concept of satisfaction.

• Option 3: "Curbed" (नियंत्रित): Restrained or kept in check; describes control, not the capacity to be satisfied.

• Option 4: "Pressing" (दबावपूर्ण): Demanding immediate action; again unrelated to the meaning of "satisfiable".

NOTE

• The prefix "in-" in "insatiable" is a negative prefix, similar to words like inedible, incurable, inevitable.

• Synonyms of "insatiable": unquenchable, voracious, greedy. Antonyms: satisfiable, content, appeasable.

question:
Identify the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in the given sentence.
Lady Stranleigh continued to smile at him brilliantly.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Dimly.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined word "brilliantly" means in a very bright, radiant or vivid manner. (चमकदार ढंग से)
◦ Example: The chandelier shone brilliantly in the hall.

• The antonym "Dimly" means in a faint, weak or unclear manner, with little light, which is directly opposite to "brilliantly".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Brightly" (चमकीले ढंग से): A near-synonym of "brilliantly", not its opposite.

• Option 3: "Cunningly" (चालाकी से): Means slyly or deceptively; unrelated to brightness or dimness.

• Option 4: "Strangely" (अजीब ढंग से): Means oddly or unusually; unrelated to the concept of brightness.

NOTE

• Other antonym pairs based on light/brightness often asked in SSC: radiant ↔ dull, luminous ↔ dark, gleaming ↔ dim, vivid ↔ faded.

question:
Select the correct spelling of the underlined word in the sentence.
Can you please come back to reality from the fectitious world you live in?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. fictitious.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "fictitious" — meaning not real or true; imaginary, invented or made-up.
◦ Example: The novel is set in a fictitious town that does not exist on any map.

• Spelling key: FIC + TI + TIOUS. The word is related to "fiction" (an invented story), and both share the root "fic-" from Latin fingere, "to shape or invent".

• The sentence contrasts "reality" with an imaginary/invented world, confirming that "fictitious" is contextually correct.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "factitious" — this is a real word, but it means artificial or contrived, made to seem genuine when it is not, which does not fit the context of an imaginary "world"; it is also not a correct spelling of the underlined word "fectitious".

• Option 2: "fractional" — means relating to a small part or fraction; unrelated in both spelling and meaning to the underlined word.

• Option 3: "factional" — means relating to a small organised group (faction) within a larger one; unrelated in both spelling and meaning.

NOTE

• Do not confuse "fictitious" (imaginary) with "factitious" (artificial/contrived) — both are correctly spelt words in English but with different meanings, and only "fictitious" fits this context.

• Related word forms: fiction (noun), fictional (adjective), fictitiously (adverb).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Purify
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Pollute.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Purify" means to make something clean by removing dirty, harmful or unwanted substances. (शुद्ध करना)
◦ Example: This machine purifies the water before it is bottled for sale.

• The antonym "Pollute" means to make something dirty or impure, especially by adding harmful substances, which is directly opposite to "purify".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Chant" (मंत्रोच्चार करना): Means to repeatedly sing or recite words; unrelated to cleanliness.

• Option 2: "Invite" (आमंत्रित करना): Means to request someone's presence; unrelated to the concept of purity.

• Option 4: "Wash" (धोना): Means to clean using water; this is actually close in meaning to "purify" and not its opposite.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "Purify": cleanse, refine, filter, decontaminate.

• Other antonyms of "Purify": contaminate, defile, taint, adulterate.

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in active voice.
Trigonometry has been taught by him for donkey's years.
option_1: He had been teaching trigonometry for donkey's years.
option_2: He has been trigonometry teaching for donkey's years.
option_3: He is teaching trigonometry for donkey's years.
option_4: He has been teaching trigonometry for donkey's years.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. He has been teaching trigonometry for donkey's years.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "Trigonometry has been taught by him for donkey's years" is in the Present Perfect Continuous Tense.

• Rule — Present Perfect Continuous Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + has/have + been + V-ing + Object
◦ Passive (as seen here): Object + has/have + been + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule in reverse: the agent "him" (introduced by "by") becomes the subject "He"; the auxiliary "has been" is retained since the subject is third person singular; the past participle "taught" is converted to its continuous form "teaching"; and "trigonometry" becomes the object.
◦ Active: He has been teaching trigonometry for donkey's years.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "had been teaching" is the active form of the Past Perfect Continuous Tense, not the Present Perfect Continuous Tense used in the original sentence.

• Option 2 is incorrect because the word order "trigonometry teaching" is grammatically wrong; the correct order is "teaching trigonometry" (verb before object).

• Option 3 is incorrect because "is teaching" is the Present Continuous Tense, not the Present Perfect Continuous Tense required here.

NOTE

• The idiom "for donkey's years" means for a very long time.

• Rule — Present Perfect Continuous Tense structure: Subject + has/have + been + V-ing + Object + since/for + time reference.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Music is perhaps the most popular and widely practised (1)_______ of fine arts, transcending all kinds of cultural and linguistic barriers.
Any form of fine art is (2)_________ to master and almost impossible to perfect, and music is no exception.
Nature, it is learnt, has blessed almost two-thirds of the human race with musical ability of some sort. Music has the power to (3)_______ out the deepest emotions. In fact, it is a magic medicine, and many seek refuge in it when they are depressed or stressed.
It is this intimacy that makes us listen to music (4)_______ even hum or sing sometimes. This singing, or realistically speaking, expressing one's emotion musically sometimes takes a serious turn.
The desire to sing before an audience is innocent and beautiful, and indeed, it is perfectly alright to have such a genuine desire. But it is also important to understand that singing is an (5)_________ art—a highly refined one at that, which requires systematic, prolonged and strict training to be acceptable.

Choose the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. form.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence states that music is "the most popular and widely practised ___ of fine arts", requiring a noun meaning a particular type, kind or variety of something.

solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. or.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "makes us listen to music ___ even hum or sing sometimes", where the blank must connect two alternative actions ("listen to music" and "hum or sing").

• "Or" is a coordinating conjunction used to present alternatives or choices, correctly linking "listen to music" with the alternative action "even hum or sing".

• Completed sentence: "It is this intimacy that makes us listen to music or even hum or sing sometimes."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "neither" is used with "nor" to negate both alternatives (neither...nor...), which does not fit this affirmative sentence.

• Option 3: "nor" is used to continue a negative statement begun with "neither" or "not"; there is no preceding negative here, so it cannot be used alone.

• Option 4: "either" is used with "or" in the correlative pair "either...or...", but the blank here is a single simple connector joining two clauses, not a correlative structure, so plain "or" is required rather than "either".

NOTE

• Correlative conjunction pairs to remember: either...or (affirmative alternatives), neither...nor (negative alternatives), not only...but also.

• Use plain "or" (without "either") when a sentence simply presents one alternative among actions already introduced, as in this passage.
